title: The friendship paradox

The same logic {{4}} why your sexual partners' partners seem busier, why co-authors have more publications than you, and why the people you follow online seem to lead richer lives. Researchers {{5}} that the effect can distort our judgement: we compare ourselves with an unusually glittering sample of humanity and find ourselves {{6}}. title: The lost art of the weekend

title: Why we talk to ourselves
text: Talking to yourself used to be a sign to worry {{1}}, but psychologists now see it as a sign of intelligence. text: The delivery app has changed the restaurant industry more quickly than anyone {{1}} have predicted a decade ago. title: Cities that never sleep?
text: Night-time economies have become a measure of urban {{1}}, and cities compete to advertise how much happens after dark. Yet researchers studying night workers tell a more complicated story. title: The comeback of the cassette
text: Music formats rarely get second {{1}}, but the cassette tape is an exception. Industry observers are cautious about the numbers: cassettes remain a rounding error compared with streaming, and much of the revival is {{4}} to collectors rather than listeners. title: Should we tax sugar?
text: When the United Kingdom introduced a tax on sugary drinks, critics predicted job losses and {{1}} protests about the nanny state. Three years later, the evidence suggests otherwise. title: The right to repair
text: When a farmer cannot repair his own tractor, or a city cannot fix its own buses, something has gone {{1}} with product design. title: What your accent says about you
text: Accent discrimination is one of the last openly tolerated prejudices, according to sociolinguists.
